dataset_family: Kaohsiung Veterans General Hospital geriatric and neurology outpatients (2019-2023) plus Gangshan and Kaohsiung Veterans Homes residents (2017-2018), Taiwan veterans-affairs health system; 237 CDR-0.5 MCI, 89 progressed to dementia over a median 34 months
method_family: Clinical longitudinal cohort: Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox regression of MCI-to-dementia progression (CDR 0.5 to 1, neurologist-confirmed), with a binary GDS-15 depressive-symptom indicator as an adjustment covariate; chi-square baseline comparison by conversion status
what_it_shows: In 237 older adults with CDR-0.5 MCI (89 progressed to CDR-1 dementia), the proportion with depressive symptoms on the GDS-15 was the same in those who progressed and those who remained MCI (14/89, 15.7% vs 24/148, 16.2%; p = 0.99), and the depressive-symptom variable did not predict progression in the multivariable Cox model (HR 0.86, 0.46-1.60, p = 0.64). Depressive symptoms are a covariate in a polypharmacy study and are reported only as n (%). The GDS-15 cut-off is not stated in the text (the assessment is detailed in Table S1, which is not in the extract).
why: Hsu et al., Alzheimers Dement (Transl Res Clin Interv) 2025;11:e70179, DOI 10.1002/trc2.70179. The PDF title, authors and DOI match the summaries.md block and the map entry. Against the Table A1 statement this is a prognosis null on depressive-symptom STATUS (a dichotomised screen), not on a continuous severity score. So it does not show that 'continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'. It shows the adjacent point that screen-positive depressive-symptom status neither separated nor predicted MCI-to-dementia progression. That is 'partly' at most. Round 1 treated presence contrasts as not being severity grading (P-989), and the same standard is applied here, although unlike P-989 this paper has no contrary continuous result. Limits: depression is an adjustment covariate and never the exposure; its cut-off is not in the extract; prevalence is low in both groups (about 16%); the cohort mixes veterans-home residents and outpatients, and recruitment source has a strong effect (HR 3.38); dementia is all-cause (CDR 1 with ICD confirmation). There are minor denominator slips in Tables 1 and 2 (58/129 printed as 45.3%, which is 58/128; polypharmacy 78 + 31 = 109 in Table 2 against 108 in Table 1), but they do not touch the depression rows. Not tested: the first clause (all participants have MCI), the brain limb and the 'although' clause. Independence: the Kaohsiung veterans-affairs cohort is not the dataset of any current supporter (Korea University Guro; Shanghai Brain Health Cohort; Shanghai Tongji; Florence) or of any round-1 or round-2 candidate, and no authors are shared. Not a preprint. Quotes are transliterated to ASCII (- for en dashes).

quotes.quote: At baseline, all participants underwent a standardized CDR assessment, and only those scoring 0.5 were classified as MCI and included in the cohort.
depressive symptoms assessed by the 15-item Chinese Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15),18

Progression from MCI to dementia was defined as an increase in the CDR score from 0.5 to 1 during follow-up. Dementia diagnoses were further confirmed by the neurologists using internationally recognized diagnostic criteria (International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision [ICD-10]21 and ICD-1122)

To examine the association between polypharmacy and dementia risk, Cox proportional hazards regression models were applied, adjusting for potential confounders, including age, sex, CCI, education, smoking status, hearing and visual impairment, Barthel Index Scores, GDS-15, MNA-SF, and recruitment source.
